concept.concept_question: Why does a backend exist at all?
What does one API call carry?
Why can’t the key live in the browser?
Why does the app forget without storage?
Why does the pointer sit on the many side?
Why is history a row, not a cell?
How do you decide where a piece lives?

case.case_scenario: A user wants to update their account subscription tier to 'Paid' via your web app. Why can't the frontend JavaScript code directly update the database row from tier: free to tier: paid?
case.case_answer: Because the client environment is untrusted; any user could modify the local client code or network payload to grant themselves paid access without executing payment logic.

case.case_scenario: An e-commerce React app calculates the cart total and applies a 90% discount code inside the browser before sending the final dollar amount directly to the payment gateway. What breaks mechanically?
case.case_answer: Because calculation happens on an untrusted client, a user can edit the local JavaScript state or intercept the network request to set the final price to $0.01 without a valid discount.

case.case_scenario: A multiplayer trivia game checks if the user's selected answer matches the correct answer inside the browser JavaScript and then sends score + 10 to the leaderboard database. How is this exploited?
case.case_answer: The correct answers are shipped inside the client bundle where users can read them in DevTools, or users can send raw HTTP requests directly incrementing their score without playing.

case.case_scenario: You want to limit free-tier users to 5 AI image generations per day by keeping a counter in browser localStorage and blocking the button after 5 clicks. Why does this fail to protect your API quota?
case.case_answer: The rate limit runs on the user's machine; a user can clear localStorage, open an incognito window, or call the endpoint directly via terminal to bypass the client-side counter.

case.case_scenario: Your frontend connects directly to a PostgreSQL database using a read-only connection string so users can view their own profile row (WHERE user_id = 5). How can User 5 read User 6's private profile?
case.case_answer: Because the query is constructed on the client, User 5 can modify the SQL query string in the browser before it executes to WHERE user_id = 6 or drop the WHERE clause entirely.

case.case_scenario: A banking web app hides the 'Approve Wire Transfer' button in the React UI using {user.isAdmin && <Button/>}. If there is no backend server checking the role, what happens when a regular user wants to approve a transfer?
case.case_answer: Hiding a UI element only affects the DOM rendering; a regular user can unhide the button in DevTools or send the underlying HTTP request directly to trigger the action without authorization.

case.case_scenario: An auction platform uses the user's browser new Date() timestamp to verify whether a bid was submitted before the 12:00 PM deadline. How can a bidder submit a winning bid at 12:05 PM?
case.case_answer: The browser reads the operating system's local clock; the user can manually roll back their computer's system time to 11:59 AM so the client generates a falsified timestamp.

case.case_scenario: A content platform blurs premium articles using CSS and relies on frontend code to strip the blur only if the user's account status is subscribed. Why can non-subscribers read the article for free?
case.case_answer: The full unredacted text of the article was already transmitted over the network into the browser DOM; anyone can open Inspect Element and delete the CSS blur class or read the raw JSON response.

case.case_scenario: Two users try to buy the last remaining concert ticket at the exact same millisecond. Why can't two separate browsers coordinate who gets the ticket without a central backend?
case.case_answer: Browsers run in isolated client environments with no shared memory or atomic locking mechanism; only a centralized server/database can serialize concurrent requests and lock the inventory row.

case.case_scenario: A file-upload form checks in JavaScript that a file ends in .png and is under 2MB before uploading it directly to a public cloud bucket. How can an attacker upload a 5GB .exe malware file?
case.case_answer: Client-side file validation only runs inside the browser UI; an attacker can bypass the browser form entirely and send a multipart HTTP POST request directly to the storage URL.

case.case_scenario: Your frontend needs to send a user's ID (42) and a new display name ('Pavan') to the server. Exactly how is this bundled and transmitted across the network socket?
case.case_answer: It is serialized into an HTTP request containing a method (PATCH/POST), a route path (/api/user), headers (Content-Type: application/json, Authorization), and a serialized JSON body payload ({"id": 42, "name": "Pavan"}).

case.case_scenario: A library app sends a request to mark a book as checked out. It includes the HTTP method and a JSON payload {"status": "checked_out"}, but has no URL or endpoint path. What is the receiving service unable to do?
case.case_answer: The server cannot locate the target resource or route handler to apply the action to, resulting in a routing failure (such as a 404 Not Found or malformed request).

case.case_scenario: A client sends an HTTP request to /api/orders/99 with valid headers and path, but omits the HTTP method (verb) entirely. What mechanical ambiguity does the server face?
case.case_answer: The server knows which resource (/api/orders/99) is targeted, but lacks the action verb (GET, DELETE, PATCH) to determine whether to read, modify, or delete that record.

case.case_scenario: Your frontend sends fetch('/api/items', { method: 'POST', body: JSON.stringify({ name: 'Book' }) }) without setting the Content-Type: application/json header. Why does the backend parser see req.body as empty or raw text?
case.case_answer: Without the Content-Type metadata header, the server does not know the byte stream in the body is JSON-formatted and fails to trigger its JSON deserialization middleware.

case.case_scenario: A user is logged in, and the frontend sends DELETE /api/posts/12 with only the method and path. Why does the server reject the request with 401 Unauthorized even though the user logged in 10 seconds ago?
case.case_answer: HTTP requests are independent and stateless; unless this specific request carries credentials in its headers (like an Authorization: Bearer token or Cookie), the server cannot identify the caller.

case.case_scenario: You try to pass a JavaScript object { count: 5 } directly over a network socket without calling JSON.stringify(). Why can't the network wire transport a live JavaScript object?
case.case_answer: A live JavaScript object is an in-memory pointer structure inside the browser's RAM; network sockets only transmit flat sequences of bytes (serialized strings/binary), requiring serialization first.

case.case_scenario: A GET /api/search request attempts to filter products by category and price range, but GET requests do not carry a body payload. Where in the API call package must those filter parameters travel?
case.case_answer: They must be encoded into the URL path's query string (e.g., /api/search?category=shoes&max_price=100) or passed via custom request headers.

case.case_scenario: The server finishes processing a POST /api/users call and sends a response back with body {"error": "Email already exists"}, but sets the HTTP status code to 200 OK. Why does the frontend's .catch() block fail to trigger?
case.case_answer: The client checks the response's numeric HTTP status code metadata (expecting 4xx/5xx for errors) before parsing the body text; a 200 status signals protocol-level success regardless of the JSON text inside.

case.case_scenario: A frontend on https://app.com calls https://api.other.com/data. The browser sends an automatic OPTIONS preflight call first. What metadata is the browser exchanging before sending the actual payload?
case.case_answer: It exchanges CORS headers (Origin, Access-Control-Allow-Origin, Access-Control-Allow-Methods) to verify if the target server permits cross-origin requests from that specific domain.

case.case_scenario: A mobile app uploads a 10MB profile photo to /api/avatar. Why does sending it as a raw binary stream with Content-Length and multipart/form-data headers work better than embedding it inside a standard URL path?
case.case_answer: URLs have strict length limits in HTTP headers/routers and only support ASCII characters, whereas the request body is designed to carry arbitrary-length binary byte chunks delineated by boundary headers.

case.case_scenario: A user opens your frontend web app, opens their browser's Network tab, and clicks a button that queries an external LLM provider. If your client-side code fetches directly with the key, what exact piece of data is exposed in plaintext?
case.case_answer: The Authorization header containing the secret Bearer token/API key, allowing anyone to copy it and replay that exact request from a terminal using curl.

case.case_scenario: A developer hides their OpenAI API key inside a minified, obfuscated JavaScript file on the frontend so users can't easily read the source code. When a user clicks 'Generate', where specifically can any user still grab the plaintext key in 5 seconds?
case.case_answer: In the browser's DevTools Network tab, because regardless of how obfuscated the code is, the browser must de-obfuscate the key in memory to attach it in plaintext to the outgoing HTTP request header.

case.case_scenario: Your teammate moves the API key out of the React code and puts it into a .env file in the frontend project using VITE_OPENAI_KEY. Why does this still expose the key to every user?
case.case_answer: Frontend build tools (like Vite or Webpack) perform static string replacement at build time, baking the .env variable directly into the public JavaScript bundle shipped to the user's browser.

case.case_scenario: A developer encrypts the API key using AES encryption and puts the encrypted ciphertext inside the frontend code, alongside the decryption key and function so the browser can use it at runtime. Why is this useless?
case.case_answer: Because both the lock (ciphertext) and the key (decryption secret/algorithm) are shipped to the same untrusted client machine, allowing any user to run the decryption function in the browser console or read the decrypted network call.

case.case_scenario: You restrict your third-party API key so it only accepts requests with the HTTP header Referer: https://your-app.com, and then put the key in your frontend code. How can an attacker still use your key from their own server?
case.case_answer: The Referer and Origin headers are only enforced by browsers; an attacker can extract the key from your frontend and run a script from a terminal or backend server where they manually spoof the Referer header.

case.case_scenario: Instead of hardcoding the key in the JavaScript bundle, your backend sends the raw OpenAI API key to the browser via a GET /api/get-secret-key call after the user logs in. Why is the key still compromised?
case.case_answer: Even if only authenticated users receive it, once the key crosses the network boundary into a user's browser, that logged-in user can inspect the /api/get-secret-key response payload and steal the master key.

case.case_scenario: A mobile app (iOS/Android) embeds a secret Stripe secret key inside its compiled binary instead of using a backend server, assuming mobile apps don't have a 'F12 Network Tab'. How is the key extracted?
case.case_answer: Users can decompile the APK/IPA binary to read hardcoded strings, or route their phone's Wi-Fi traffic through a local MITM proxy (like Charles Proxy or Wireshark) to inspect the outgoing HTTP headers.

case.case_scenario: A developer stores the API key in an HttpOnly cookie thinking JavaScript can't read it, and tells the browser to call api.openai.com directly. Why does this fail both mechanically and security-wise?
case.case_answer: HttpOnly cookies are only sent automatically to the domain that set them (not third-party APIs requiring an Authorization: Bearer header), and any cookie sent by the browser is still visible in the user's own DevTools Network/Application tab.
case_answer_kw_synonym: client can still read own cookies

case.case_scenario: You push your frontend code containing the API key to a private GitHub repository and deploy it to Vercel. Even though the repo is private, how can a random visitor on your live website get the key?
case.case_answer: A private Git repo only hides the source code before deployment; once deployed, Vercel serves the compiled JavaScript files publicly over HTTP to any browser that visits the URL.
case_answer_kw_synonym: private repo doesn't hide client code

case.case_scenario: Your frontend uses a Firebase/Supabase key directly in the browser. When is a client-side key actually safe to expose in the browser?
case.case_answer: Only when it is a public/anon identifier paired with strict server-side Row Level Security (RLS) rules, meaning the key itself grants zero administrative privileges and the backend database enforces per-user permissions.

case.case_scenario: A user fills out a multi-step form, reaches step 3, and accidentally refreshes the browser tab. Why does the form reset to step 1 if you haven't written code for database or local storage?
case.case_answer: The browser tab's RAM wiped the active execution context upon reloading, destroying all JavaScript state variables that existed only in volatile memory.

case.case_scenario: Your Node.js backend stores all newly registered users inside a global array const users = []. When you deploy a tiny bug fix and the server process restarts, why can't any existing user log in?
case.case_answer: The users array lived in the Node.js process's volatile RAM; terminating and restarting the OS process deallocates that memory space, wiping the array back to [] because nothing was written to non-volatile disk.

case.case_scenario: Inside an Express route handler app.post('/count', (req, res) => { let count = 0; count++; }), why does every single API call return 1 instead of incrementing 2, 3, 4?
case.case_answer: Local variables declared inside a function are allocated on the call stack when the request starts and garbage-collected the moment the function returns the response.

case.case_scenario: You move let count = 0 to the top of your backend file (global memory) and run 4 instances of your server behind a load balancer. Why does a user see the counter jump randomly between 1, 4, and 2 on consecutive refreshes?
case.case_answer: Each server instance runs in its own isolated OS process with separate RAM; without a shared external storage layer (like Redis or a database), each process only increments its own private in-memory variable.

case.case_scenario: A serverless function (like AWS Lambda or Vercel Functions) stores a user's session in a global variable. Why does the session randomly disappear after 10 minutes of inactivity?
case.case_answer: Serverless environments freeze and spin down idle containers to save compute resources, deallocating the container's RAM; the next request triggers a cold start with a brand-new memory space.

case.case_scenario: A user adds 3 items to their shopping cart stored in React useState([]), then copies the URL and pastes it into a new browser tab. Why is the cart empty in the new tab?
case.case_answer: React useState allocates memory strictly inside the isolated JavaScript heap of the first browser tab; a new tab spawns a completely separate process and memory space with no access to the first tab's RAM.

case.case_scenario: Your backend writes uploaded files to the container's local /tmp folder on Render or Heroku. Why do all user avatars vanish the next day even though fs.writeFileSync wrote them to a file path?
case.case_answer: Cloud containers use an ephemeral filesystem that is recreated from the base build image on every deploy or daily container cycle, wiping any files not sent to persistent object storage (like S3) or a mounted volume.

case.case_scenario: A React component fetches a list of comments and stores them in component state. When the user clicks to the 'Profile' tab and clicks back to 'Comments', why did the comments disappear until a new fetch ran?
case.case_answer: Unmounting the React component destroys its instance in the virtual DOM and garbage-collects its local state hook memory from RAM.

case.case_scenario: You run a SQLite database configured with :memory: mode during testing. What happens to all inserted rows the microsecond your test script finishes executing?
case.case_answer: SQLite :memory: creates the tables entirely inside the process's volatile RAM rather than flushing pages to a .db file on disk, so OS memory reclamation erases the database upon process exit.
case_answer_kw_synonym: no file written to hard drive

case.case_scenario: A user types a long essay into an HTML <textarea> without any JavaScript attached, and their laptop battery suddenly dies. Why is the text gone when they boot back up?
case.case_answer: The typed characters were held exclusively in the browser's volatile DOM memory inside physical RAM, which requires continuous electrical current to maintain its state and vanishes on power loss.

case.case_scenario: You are modeling a school system where a Student can enroll in multiple Courses, and each Course can have multiple Students. Where do you put the pointer column?
case.case_answer: You cannot put it directly on either table because it is a many-to-many relationship; you must create a third junction table (e.g., Enrollments) where each row holds two foreign key pointers referencing one student_id and one course_id.

case.case_scenario: One Author writes many Books, and each Book has only one Author. If you put a book_id column on the Authors table instead of author_id on Books, what happens when an author publishes their second book?
case.case_answer: Either the single book_id cell on the Authors row must hold multiple values ('101, 102'), violating atomic column rules, or you must duplicate the entire Author row for every new book they write.
case_answer_kw_synonym: cannot hold multiple keys in one scalar field

case.case_scenario: In your Concept Check app, one initial learning Gap (attempt 1) can have multiple Retries (attempts 2, 3). Why does the parent_gap_id foreign key column sit on the Retries table instead of a retry_id column on the Gaps table?
case.case_answer: Because each retry points back to exactly one single parent gap (an atomic value), whereas a single gap row would have to store an unbounded list of retry IDs as the learner makes more attempts.
case_answer_kw_synonym: each retry has exactly one gap
gap would need multiple retry ids
single scalar pointer on many side

case.case_scenario: A Department has 50 Employees. A developer puts columns emp1_id, emp2_id, ... emp10_id on the Departments table. What breaks when the department hires an 11th employee?
case.case_answer: The table schema hits a hard structural ceiling, requiring an ALTER TABLE DDL migration just to insert data, whereas putting department_id on the Employees table allows infinite employees by simply inserting new rows.
case_answer_kw_synonym: alter table needed for new data
many side adds rows without changing columns

case.case_scenario: A Customer places multiple Orders. You store a comma-separated string 'ord_1, ord_2, ord_3' inside a single order_ids column on the Customers table. What breaks when you try to enforce a database FOREIGN KEY constraint or join the tables?
case.case_answer: Relational database engines cannot enforce foreign key referential integrity or use B-tree indexes on substrings inside a comma-separated text field, making standard SQL joins and cascading deletes impossible.
case_answer_kw_synonym: no referential integrity on csv string
database cannot validate multiple ids in text

case.case_scenario: A Blog Post has many Comments. If you put comment_id on the Posts table and duplicate the Posts row for every new comment so each row stays atomic, what breaks when the author edits the Post's title?
case.case_answer: You suffer an update anomaly: the database must find and update the title across hundreds of duplicated Post rows, risking inconsistent data if any row fails to update.
case_answer_kw_synonym: must update title in multiple places

case.case_scenario: Using the same duplicated Posts table (where comment_id lives on the Posts row), what happens if a post has only 1 comment and the user deletes that comment row?
case.case_answer: If deleting the comment deletes the row holding the comment_id pointer, you suffer a deletion anomaly where the entire Blog Post record is accidentally wiped out along with its last comment.
case_answer_kw_synonym: cannot exist with zero comments or requires null mutation

case.case_scenario: A Folder contains many Files, and each File lives in exactly one Folder. If a File is moved from Folder A to Folder B, how many database rows must be modified if folder_id is on the Files table versus if file_ids arrays are stored on Folders?
case.case_answer: With folder_id on Files (the many side), moving a file is an atomic single-row update (SET folder_id = 'B'); on the Folders side, you must mutate two separate rows (removing from A's array and appending to B's array).
case_answer_kw_synonym: update one cell on child row
modify both source and destination folder rows
risk of file existing in two folders simultaneously

case.case_scenario: An Invoice has many Line Items. You want to calculate the sum of all line item prices for Invoice #10. Why is SELECT SUM(price) FROM line_items WHERE invoice_id = 10 fast when the pointer is on line_items?
case.case_answer: Because invoice_id sits as a scalar column on the line_items table, the database can use a B-tree index on invoice_id to jump directly to the matching child rows in O(log N) time.

case.case_scenario: In a self-referencing Employees table where one Manager manages many Direct Reports, which employee row holds the manager_id pointer column, and what value does it hold?
case.case_answer: Every Employee row (the 'many' side) holds a single manager_id column pointing to the id of their one Manager; a Manager has many rows pointing to them, while holding only one manager_id for their own boss.

case.case_scenario: You want to track a learner's first failed attempt alongside their second successful attempt for a specific concept check. Why does updating a single text column (latest_attempt) break your ability to analyze their learning gap?
case.case_answer: Overwriting the cell destroys the initial failed attempt data, meaning you lose the record of what they originally got wrong and cannot link their retry directly to the specific gap.
case_answer_kw_synonym: cannot point foreign key to previous state

case.case_scenario: Instead of overwriting, a developer appends every new attempt into a single text cell separated by pipes ('Attempt 1 | Attempt 2 | Attempt 3'). What breaks when you need to record the exact timestamp and pass/fail boolean for Attempt 2?
case.case_answer: A single concatenated text cell cannot attach independent structured metadata columns (created_at, passed, parent_gap_id) or primary keys to individual events inside the string.

case.case_scenario: A bank stores a user's account balance in a single mutable cell balance = 500 and overwrites it to balance = 400 on withdrawal without inserting a transaction row. Why can't the bank prove where the missing $100 went during a dispute?
case.case_answer: Mutating the cell in place records only the final net state while erasing the causal transition event (who received the $100, when it occurred, and what the prior balance was).
case_answer_kw_synonym: impossible to reconstruct timeline or verify math

case.case_scenario: Two webhook events arrive at the exact same millisecond and both try to append a status update to a single JSON array cell inside the Orders row (UPDATE orders SET history = ...). What concurrency bug occurs?
case.case_answer: Both requests read the same initial cell value, append their item in memory, and write back—causing a lost update race condition where the second write completely overwrites the first webhook's addition.
case_answer_kw_synonym: insert row avoids overwriting existing data

case.case_scenario: You want to query 'How many learners failed on their first try between 2:00 PM and 3:00 PM today?' Why is this query trivial when attempts are rows, but requires a full-table scan when history is stored in a JSON/text cell?
case.case_answer: When attempts are rows, the database uses an index on the created_at and attempt_number columns; inside a cell, the engine must load and parse every user's text blob in the entire table to inspect internal values.

case.case_scenario: In your Concept Check app, Attempt 3 is a retry that fixes a specific sentence flagged in Attempt 1. Why can't Attempt 3 hold a foreign key pointer (parent_gap_id) to Attempt 1 if all attempts are stored inside a single cell on the Users table?
case.case_answer: Foreign keys can only reference a unique Primary Key of a discrete table row; an item buried inside a text or array cell has no table-level primary key to point to.
case_answer_kw_synonym: foreign key points to row pk

case.case_scenario: An e-commerce site stores an order's shipping status in a single cell status that gets overwritten from placed -> packed -> shipped -> delivered. Why can't you calculate the average time it takes for the warehouse to pack an order?
case.case_answer: Overwriting the single status (and updated_at) cell destroys the timestamp of when placed transitioned to packed the moment shipped overwrites it, eliminating the time delta between intermediate steps.

case.case_scenario: A user edits their document 1,000 times, and you append every full revision into a single revision_history column on the Documents row. How does this degrade SELECT id, title FROM documents queries that don't even need the history?
case.case_answer: Bloating a single row with a massive growing cell forces the database storage engine to read across oversized data/TOAST pages, slowing down row fetches and consuming memory/locks on the main record.

case.case_scenario: A bug in your code accidentally corrupts the latest status update. If history is stored by inserting immutable append-only rows versus mutating a single cell, how do you recover the user's state from 5 minutes ago?
case.case_answer: With append-only rows, prior rows remain untouched so you simply delete the bad row or query WHERE created_at < '5 mins ago'; with a mutated cell, the prior value was overwritten in place and is unrecoverable without a full DB backup restore.
case_answer_kw_synonym: previous state still exists as separate row
overwritten cell permanently destroys old value

case.case_scenario: A SaaS app lets users change their subscription plan. If you overwrite plan_id on the Users row instead of inserting a subscription_events row with start_date and end_date, what breaks when generating last month's invoice after a user upgrades mid-month?
case.case_answer: You only know their current plan today and have lost the historical record of which days they were on the cheaper plan versus the upgraded plan during the billing cycle.
case_answer_kw_synonym: missing start_date and end_date per plan

case.case_scenario: You are building a feature that validates whether a password meets complexity requirements before submission. Should this validation logic run exclusively on the server, or on the client (or both), and why?
case.case_answer: It should run on the client for immediate UX feedback without network latency, but must also run on the server because client-side validation is untrusted and can be bypassed by sending a raw API request.

case.case_scenario: As a user drags a color-picker slider at 60 frames per second, you want the preview box on screen to update its background color smoothly. Why must this state live on the client instead of making an API call to the backend on every pixel movement?
case.case_answer: Round-trip network latency (50–200ms per HTTP call) is far slower than the 16.6ms frame budget required for 60fps UI rendering, which would cause severe visual lag and flood the server.
case_answer_kw_synonym: no trust boundary needed for visual preview

case.case_scenario: In your Concept Check app, where must the grading comparison against the Known Answer Key live—in the frontend React code or on the backend server—and what breaks if you put it in the other place?
case.case_answer: It must live on the backend server; if the Known Answer Key is shipped to the frontend to grade locally, any learner can inspect the client bundle or network tab to read the exact answers before typing.
case_answer_kw_synonym: shipping rubric to browser leaks answers

case.case_scenario: You have an e-commerce catalog of 5,000,000 products and need to filter them down to the 10 cheapest items matching a search keyword. Why should this filtering live in the database query rather than fetching all rows to the browser .filter()?
case.case_answer: Shipping 5 million rows over the network consumes hundreds of megabytes of bandwidth and crashes the browser's RAM, whereas the database sits next to the disk and uses memory-efficient B-tree indexes to return only 10 rows.
case_answer_kw_synonym: db filters via index before network serialization

case.case_scenario: A user toggles 'Dark Mode' on a documentation website that doesn't require an account login. Why is browser localStorage a better place for this piece of state than a backend PostgreSQL database?
case.case_answer: Dark mode is a non-sensitive, device-local UI preference with zero security risk if tampered with, and reading it synchronously from localStorage prevents a flash of unstyled white content before a network call completes.

case.case_scenario: A user is editing a profile modal and opens a dropdown menu (isOpen = true). Why should isOpen live in ephemeral React state (RAM) rather than being saved to localStorage or the backend database?
case.case_answer: Whether a dropdown is currently open is transient view state tied only to the current interaction moment; persisting it to storage adds pointless I/O overhead and causes annoying UI bugs if the modal reopens unexpectedly after a page refresh.

case.case_scenario: A medical app needs to run a 4GB machine learning model that requires 16GB of VRAM to analyze an X-ray image. Why must this execution live on the backend server rather than inside the user's mobile browser?
case.case_answer: Execution environment constraints: a mobile browser sandbox lacks the gigabytes of RAM/GPU hardware required and cannot force every user to download a 4GB model weight file over cellular data.
case_answer_kw_synonym: centralized server hardware handles heavy compute

case.case_scenario: An online multiplayer poker game needs to shuffle a deck of 52 cards and deal 2 hidden cards to Player A and 2 hidden cards to Player B. Where must the deck array and shuffle algorithm live, and what breaks if the server sends the full shuffled deck array to both browsers?
case.case_answer: The deck and shuffle must live exclusively on the backend server, with the server sending each client only their own 2 cards; sending the full deck array to the browser lets any player inspect network traffic to see their opponent's hidden cards and upcoming river cards.
case_answer_kw_synonym: full deck in browser leaks opponent's hand in devtools

case.case_scenario: A user types into a live character counter (142 / 280 characters) while composing a post. Why should the character counting logic run on the client, while the final length rejection runs on the server?
case.case_answer: Counting characters on the client gives instant keystroke-by-keystroke visual feedback with zero network latency, while the server must re-verify text.length <= 280 on submission so a user cannot POST a 10,000-character string via curl.
case_answer_kw_synonym: raw api request can bypass frontend input maxlength

case.case_scenario: Your app generates a downloadable PDF invoice stamped with 'OFFICIAL PAID RECEIPT' once Stripe confirms payment. Why must the Stripe webhook listener and PDF stamp generation live on the backend rather than awaiting Stripe's redirect in the browser?
case.case_answer: A user can close their browser tab before the redirect completes (losing the event) or manually visit the /payment-success redirect URL in their browser without paying to forge a receipt; only the backend can cryptographically verify Stripe's webhook signature secret.
case_answer_kw_synonym: user can visit success url directly without paying
reliable background processing even if client disconnects
